lesson.title: hay: The Universal Existence
lesson.subtitle: hay un problema, ¿hay café?, no hay nada — existence independent of number

hook.title: One Word for Singular and Plural
hook.content: In English, you must choose between 'there is a table' and 'there are three tables'. In Spanish, hay never changes! Hay una mesa ('There is a table') and Hay tres mesas ('There are three tables') both use hay.

pattern.title: Greek -ma Nouns: Why It Is 'Un Problema'
pattern.content: Look at el problema ('the problem'). Even though it ends in -a, it came into Latin from Greek neuter nouns in -ma (el problema, el sistema, el programa, el tema, el clima), which are all MASCULINE in Spanish: hay un problema!

exercises.prompt: Match each English expression with its Spanish partner:
exercises.target_answer: hay, un problema, no hay nada, no hay nadie, ¿hay café?, aquí
exercises.meaning: there is / there are, a problem (masculine!), there isn't anything, there is nobody, is there coffee?, here
exercises.explanation: hay handles both singular and plural; el/un problema is masculine.

exercises.prompt: Why do we say 'Hay UN problema' instead of *una problema?
options: Greek nouns ending in -ma (problema, sistema, programa) are masculine in Spanish
Because problema ends in a consonant
exercises.target_answer: Greek nouns ending in -ma (problema, sistema, programa) are masculine in Spanish
exercises.explanation: Words of Greek origin ending in -ma take el / un: el problema, un problema.

exercises.prompt: Assemble: 'There is a good restaurant here'
exercises.meaning: There is a good restaurant here
exercises.explanation: Hay ('There is') + un restaurante bueno + aquí.

exercises.idea: say that there is nobody here
exercises.explanation: No hay nadie aquí — double negation with hay + nadie.

exercises.prompt: Listen and write the whole sentence.
exercises.affirmation: You caught both silent-h hay and masculine un problema!

summary.outcome: Use hay for singular and plural existence and treat Greek -ma nouns like problema as masculine.

use_example.german: ¿Hay café? — No, no hay nada aquí.
use_example.english: Is there coffee? — No, there is nothing here.

summary.takeaway: Use estar for the location of a specific thing (El café está aquí) and hay for general existence (Hay café aquí).

hay.etymology_derivation: Latin habet ('it has') + Old Spanish y ('there', Latin ibi). Identical structure to French il y a.

problema.etymology_derivation: Greek nouns ending in -ma (el problema, el sistema, el programa, el tema, el clima) are MASCULINE despite ending in -a!

café.etymology_derivation: Turkish kahve → Italian caffè → Spanish café. An international word shared across Europe.

mesa.context_translation: I want to reserve a table.
mesa.etymology_derivation: Latin mēnsa ('table') gave Spanish la mesa — which English borrowed in the American Southwest for a flat-topped 'table' mountain!

nada.context_translation: I want nothing (I don't want anything).
nada.etymology_derivation: Latin rēs nāta ('born thing'). In Spanish, double negation reinforces: no quiero nada.

nadie.etymology_derivation: Reinforces no in Spanish double negation.
